source.title: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility
source.authors: S. Regmi; Siddhartha Pudasaini; Chetan Phakami Pun

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports compute using Kaplan et al.'s 6ND estimate, but does not test scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations. Its own tokenizer and held-out-loss results are adjacent findings, not tests of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-model held-out bits-per-byte for three tokenizer/training conditions. These results do not measure scaling-law behavior, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture effects, other modalities, downstream-task predictability, or fitted-law dependence. It also cites scaling-law work and uses the 6ND estimate to report FLOPs; cited results themselves are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper studies a pre-tokenizer regex defect and its effect on fertility and held-out bits per byte at one model scale (268M). It cites Kaplan et al. only to estimate FLOPs via 6ND. There is no variation in parameters, tokens or compute fitted to a power law, no extrapolation, no allocation study, no architecture sweep and no downstream-task scaling, so no version is tested. T4 fits better than T6 because the 6ND estimate from the original is used as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. One addition: the authors also report that English bits per byte improves 1.84% despite a 2.1% English fertility cost. The paper's main conclusions concern a training-free fertility floor, the mixture-sweep diagnostic, script coverage and a HuggingFace census, not model scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares tokenizer character classes and does not apply the original scaling-law measurement or fitting recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Tokenizer character class and token budget differ across the reported runs; the paper also notes a single seed per downstream condition.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal token budget, a 268M model with a mark-aware tokenizer reaches 4.43% lower held-out Nepali bits per byte (0.3899 vs 0.4080). It still beats the broken-tokenizer model given the same bytes at 1.59× compute (0.3925), on one seed. On English, C leads B, ordering by compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-tokenizer choice can shift held-out bits per byte by more than a 1.59× compute increase, for abugida-script languages.

record.problems: The held-out model comparison uses one seed per condition, one model scale, and one language pair; the paper reports no error bars and notes that the small Run B–Run C difference is too thin to defend on its own. It does not test scaling-law fits or extrapolations.

untested.parts: All: no sweep of parameters, tokens or compute across orders of magnitude.
All: a single architecture (16 layers, d_model 1024).
All: the paper reports bits per byte and states no task accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: English held-out values are not recorded as rows: A 1.1706, B 1.1490, C 1.1342. They are irrelevant to any version but complete Table 5. The Kaplan citation is used only to estimate FLOPs (2.3e19).

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute across several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities and training regimes.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss; the paper measures held-out bits per byte, not downstream-task performance.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Run A
rows.operation_detail: Trained with the broken tokenizer for 4.00B tokens; held-out evaluation reported in bits per byte.
rows.uncertainty: not stated; the paper says one seed per condition and no error bars
rows.note: One of three runs sharing a 268M-parameter architecture; serves as the broken-tokenizer equal-token-budget condition.
rows.check: A single-scale loss value for a tokenizer condition. It cannot show any scaling-law effect. The compute condition 'not stated for this run' is inaccurate: Run A uses the same 4.00B-token budget as Run B, at equal compute.

rows.subject: Run B
rows.operation_detail: Trained with the fixed tokenizer for 4.00B tokens; held-out evaluation reported in bits per byte.
rows.uncertainty: not stated; the paper says one seed per condition and no error bars
rows.note: The paper reports a 4.43% improvement over Run A at equal compute.
rows.check: Tokenizer comparison at fixed scale, with no bearing on a version. The compute condition value '4.00B budget' should read 'equal to Run A'.

rows.subject: Run C
rows.operation_detail: Trained with the broken tokenizer for enough tokens to read the same bytes as Run B; held-out evaluation reported in bits per byte.
rows.uncertainty: not stated; the paper says one seed per condition and no error bars
rows.note: The paper describes the Run B–Run C gap as 0.65% on a single seed and says it is too thin to defend on its own.
rows.check: Has 1.59× more tokens than B but a different tokenizer. This is not a token-scaling measurement, and two points cannot show a power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
